reader.summary: The dominant story this week was the intensification of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Houthis launched multiple missile and drone barrages targeting Riyadh, Mecca, and the oil-rich Eastern Region, hitting the Ras Tanura refinery and striking Riyadh Airport repeatedly. Saudi air defenses intercepted numerous projectiles, and the Saudi-led coalition destroyed Houthi missile facilities in Yemen, killing 14 at a market in northern Yemen. The attacks grounded flights, forced Riyadh Airport to close and then partially reopen, and sent oil prices swinging. Diplomatically, Iran hosted Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani officials in Tehran for peace talks, with all sides agreeing to continue negotiations. Egypt's parliament authorized military support for Saudi Arabia to defend against Houthi attacks. The US ordered non-emergency embassy staff to leave the kingdom, signaling elevated security concerns. Economically, Saudi oil exports hit wartime highs as Aramco ramped up shipments, and the kingdom agreed to store oil in Singapore caverns from 2027. The 2027 Dakar Rally was moved out of Saudi Arabia, and the 2027 Asian Cup schedule was confirmed. Russian satellites were reported to be helping Houthis target Saudi facilities, adding a new dimension to the conflict.

display.eli5:
Right now, Yemen's Houthi rebels are launching waves of missiles and drones at Saudi cities like Riyadh and Mecca, and at oil refineries. Saudi air defenses are shooting most of them down, but some get through and cause damage. This has been going on for weeks and is getting worse.

At the same time, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Turkey, and Pakistan met in Tehran to try to talk the conflict down. They all said the talks went well and agreed to keep meeting. Next week, we should see what concrete steps they actually agree on, like a plan to reduce Houthi attacks. This is the Tehran peace talks follow-up.

The US is watching closely and has already told its embassy staff to leave. Expect Washington to send more military hardware, like air-defense systems, to help protect Saudi Arabia. Oil prices will keep bouncing up and down depending on whether the attacks get worse or the peace talks make progress.

A surprise would be Saudi Arabia announcing a big new purchase of AI-powered missile defense technology from a Western country, which would be a direct response to the gaps the Houthis have been exploiting.

During the week of October 17-24, 2026, Saudi Arabia endured its most intense Houthi attack campaign to date. Yemen's Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones at multiple Saudi cities, killing at least three people at the Dammam airport and an Aramco oil field in the Eastern Region. The Saudi-led coalition intercepted several waves but could not stop all strikes. The United States ordered some embassy staff and diplomats to depart, and the United Kingdom deployed Typhoon fighter jets for defensive air patrols over Saudi cities. Aramco ordered the evacuation of its Dhahran headquarters and asked staff to work remotely. The kingdom postponed its flagship 'Davos in the Desert' investor conference to 2027, and airlines canceled or restricted flights to Riyadh. Egypt's President Sisi sought parliamentary authorization to provide military support to Saudi Arabia, with the vote delayed to October 26. Turkey moved to ratify the Mecca Defense Pact with Pakistan
